rv.q: Scenery is struck and replaced within abriefwhisk ofthe revolve. One moment we are in an office, the next ithas been turned into a fairground carousel. Add train interiors, acountry house, a New York office, a dingy flat, and more - plus a blaze.

This has, as I say, a more classical antecedent, but Warner makes it work beautifully. Huston and director Robert Allan Ackerman also settle on a more recent allusion, which is again borne out by the material: once you have Bruno pinned as an effete, alcoholic southern momma's boy, it is entirely natural that he should look like Tennessee Williams.

Thrillers onceflourished intheWest End but in recent years they have gone out of fashion. All we have been left with is the mouldy old Mousetrap, not so much a playas a pieceoftheatrical archaeology,and the long running (and genuinely scary) The Woman in Black.
There was me worrying that this new stage version ofStrangers on a Train would tum out to be one of those skilful but pointlessly faithful rehashes ofa great film.

Alert to the scope for a solution that satisfies both ofthem, Bruno suggests they swap victims - a proposal that entangles them in a web ofanxiety. Robert Allan Ackerman's production is stylish yet feels under-powered.
